questions.q: Which type is the top type: every value can be assigned to it, and you must check a value before using it?
questions.explain: unknown is the set of all values. any also accepts every value, but it then lets you do anything with it, which is not a place in the hierarchy but an exit from checking.

questions.q: Which statement about never is true?
questions.explain: never is the bottom type. Adding the empty set to a union changes nothing, which is why it vanishes there.
options: Any value can be assigned to it
It is the empty set: no value can be assigned to it, and it disappears from unions (string | never is string)

questions.q: Why is any described as "an exit from the type system" rather than a place in it?
questions.explain: An any value goes into a number parameter, has any method called on it, and passes any on to whatever it touches. The compiler stops checking.
options: Because it only exists at runtime
Because everything can be assigned to it and it can be assigned to everything, so no check happens in either direction
Because it is the same as unknown

questions.q: Why did credit(event.data.walletId, event.data.amount) compile, when credit takes amount: number and the JSON held the string "5000"?
questions.explain: The compiler never saw the JSON text; JSON.parse is declared to return any. Annotate the result as unknown to force checks.
options: Because strict mode is off for JSON
Because JSON.parse returns any, every property read from it is any, and any is accepted by a number parameter
Because TypeScript converts the string to a number

questions.q: Which any does strict (noImplicitAny) report?
questions.explain: noImplicitAny only catches any the compiler would have to invent (TS7006). An any that comes from a declaration, or that you write yourself, is explicit and accepted without a word.
options: A parameter with no type and no context: function total(items) { … }

questions.q: What is the inferred return type of this function, and why does it matter?
questions.explain: any spreads through property reads and return values. A caller far away gets any silently. Annotate the parse as unknown, or give the function a checked return type.
options: any; every caller, in any file, receives an unchecked value without ever seeing JSON.parse

questions.q: Given const event: unknown = JSON.parse(body), which line compiles?
questions.explain: An unknown value can only be checked, stored or passed on as unknown. Reading properties, calling methods and passing it as a number are refused (TS18046, TS2345) until you narrow.

questions.q: Which of these is not a boundary where data should enter as unknown?
questions.explain: A boundary is where data comes from outside the compiler's view: the network, disk, the database, other services. Your own typed functions are inside it.
options: A row returned from the database
A message read from a queue
The return value of a function in your own module whose return type is annotated and checked by tsc

questions.q: With strict on, what is the type of error in catch (error) { … }, and why?
questions.explain: The useUnknownInCatchVariables flag (part of strict) makes it unknown. Check with error instanceof Error before reading error.message.
options: Error, because only errors can be thrown
unknown, because JavaScript can throw any value: strings, numbers, undefined
never, because the catch block cannot run

questions.q: A test deliberately passes a string where a number is expected, to check that the function rejects it. Which spelling is the least bad?
questions.explain: The double assertion says out loud that the test is lying on purpose, and nothing else in the file becomes any. // @ts-expect-error on that line would also work, and would fail if the parameter were ever loosened.
options: Turn off strict for the test file

questions.q: What does the return type never on function fail(message: string): never let TypeScript do?
questions.explain: A function that never returns ends that path. After if (balance === undefined) fail(…), balance can only be a number.
options: Know that code after a call to fail cannot run, so it can narrow types after if (x === undefined) fail(…)

questions.q: Why does const cart = { items: [] }; cart.items.push({ sku: "RICE-5KG" }); report that the argument is not assignable to never?
questions.explain: Give the empty container a type, for example an interface with items: CartItem[]. The same rule as always: annotate empty containers.
options: Because an empty array literal inside an object has nothing to infer from, so its type is never[], an array that can hold nothing

questions.q: What does TypeScript say about item.price when item has type never?
questions.explain: The empty type has no properties. You usually see this error as a follow-on from a never[] array: its elements are never, so every property read fails.
options: TS2339: Property 'price' does not exist on type 'never'

questions.q: What happens with function logTransfer(ref: string): void { return ref.length; }?
questions.explain: On a function you declare, : void means "returns nothing", and the compiler holds the body to it.
options: It compiles; void accepts any return value
Error: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'void'
It compiles, and callers receive the length

questions.q: Why is const remember: (ref: string) => void = (ref) => sent.push(ref); allowed, although push returns a number?
questions.explain: This is what lets you pass (x) => list.push(x) to forEach. The result's type is void, so you cannot use it as a number later.
options: Because on a function type, void means "the result will be ignored", so a function that returns something may be used there
Because arrow functions cannot return values

questions.q: Why does payouts.forEach(async (p) => { await pay(p); }) compile, even though nothing waits for the payouts?
questions.explain: By the rules of void the code is correct, so only a linter (no-misused-promises) can catch it. Use for…of with await, or await Promise.all(payouts.map(…)).
options: Because forEach's callback returns void, and a function returning a promise is allowed where the result is ignored
Because await is not checked inside callbacks

questions.q: Which value can be assigned to the lowercase type object?
questions.explain: object means any non-primitive: plain objects, arrays, functions, dates, maps. Numbers, strings and null are not objects.

questions.q: What does the type {} accept?
questions.explain: {} is an object type with no required properties, so any value that is not null or undefined fits, even 42. A parameter data: {} accepts save(42).
options: Any value except null and undefined, including numbers and strings

questions.q: Should you write Object (capital O) as a parameter type?
questions.explain: Like String, Number and Boolean, the capitalised Object is the type of a built-in JavaScript object, not what you mean in a signature.
options: Yes, it is the precise type for plain objects
No: it behaves almost like {} and accepts primitives too; use unknown, Record<string, unknown> or a real interface

questions.q: Which value is rejected by Record<string, unknown>?
questions.explain: An array type has no string index signature, so it does not fit. Record<string, unknown> is a good type for "a plain object with unchecked values", which is exactly what a JSON object is before you check it.

questions.q: When is the lowercase object type the right choice?
questions.explain: It is rare, but real: some APIs need "any non-primitive". For data you will read properties from, prefer a real interface or Record<string, unknown>.
options: When the value must not be a primitive, for example a key in a WeakMap, which only accepts objects

questions.q: The compiler accepts an explicit any silently. What finds every place one is used?
questions.explain: The no-unsafe-assignment, no-unsafe-member-access, no-unsafe-call and no-unsafe-return rules report where an any flows, which tsc never does.
options: A linter, such as typescript-eslint's no-explicit-any and no-unsafe-* rules

questions.q: A type test says // @ts-expect-error above const x: string = parseEvent("{}");. What does it detect?
questions.explain: With a real result type, assigning to string is an error, as expected. If the result ever becomes any, it becomes assignable, and tsc reports TS2578.
options: That parseEvent has started returning any: an any fits string, so the expected error disappears and the unused directive fails the check
Nothing; the directive hides all errors

questions.explain: event.amount is any, so the string reaches credit. 10000 + "2500" joins text: "100002500".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: * always converts to numbers, so doubled is 5000. + with a string joins text. That difference is why an any amount can look right in one place and be wrong in the next.

questions.explain: A TypeError is an Error, so the first branch runs and prints the message. A thrown string and a thrown undefined are not errors; that is why catch gives you unknown.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: For W2, fail throws, so balance * 2 never runs with undefined. Because fail returns never, TypeScript also knew balance was a number on the last line.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: forEach starts both callbacks and returns without waiting, so done prints first. The payments finish afterwards. The compiler allowed it because the callback's result is void.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.all waits for every promise and keeps the results in the same order as the input, so the summary comes last.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A function that returns something may be used where the result is ignored, so the assignment is fine and both pushes happen.
options: It does not compile: push returns a number

questions.q: This compiles, because the parameter type is {}. What does it print?
questions.explain: {} accepts every value except null and undefined, so a number and a string were saved as "data". A real interface would have refused them.
options: It does not compile: 42 is not an object

questions.q: Make readTopUp safe: parse into unknown, check that walletId is a string and amount a positive whole number, and return either the checked object or an error string. Print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: Annotating the parse as unknown stops any at the door. Each check narrows the type, and the returned object is built only from checked values.

questions.q: Write describeError(error: unknown): string that returns the message for an Error, the text for a thrown string, and "unknown error" for anything else. Print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: catch gives you unknown because anything can be thrown. instanceof Error and typeof narrow it before you read anything.

questions.q: Give the cart a type so its empty items array can receive items, then print the total 15100.
questions.explain: Without a type, items: [] is never[] and every push is refused. The annotation gives the empty array an element type.

questions.q: The summary prints before the messages are sent. Fix it so all messages are sent (at the same time) and 3 sent prints last.
questions.explain: forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, which void allows. Promise.all waits for all of them.
questions.expected:
sms to 0803
sms to 0805
sms to 0807
3 sent

questions.q: Write fail(message: string): never and use it in limitFor so that, after the check, TypeScript knows the limit is a number. Print 100000 and then the error message for tier "platinum".
questions.explain: The starter's ?? 0 silently gave unknown tiers a limit of zero. fail returns never, so after the if, limit is a number, and an unknown tier is a loud error.

questions.q: Write isRecord(value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown> that is true only for non-null, non-array objects, and print the results for an object, an array, null and a string.
questions.explain: typeof null and typeof [] are both "object", which is why the starter says true for them. The value is … return type makes the function a type guard, so callers can read properties (as unknown) after checking.

questions.q: Replace the {} parameter type with an interface Receipt (reference: string, kobo: number) so numbers and strings can no longer be saved. Print the saved receipt.
questions.explain: {} accepts every value except null and undefined. A real interface says what data is, and save(42) becomes a compile error.
